messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 29
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Dancer
- Trauma Type: Terrorism
- Pcl5: 69

At twenty-nine, she makes her living through movement. Before the bombing, her life is organized around rehearsal schedules, auditions, side jobs teaching children’s classes, and the quiet private rituals that keep a dancer’s body working: stretching on the studio floor before sunrise, wrapping sore ankles, counting music in her head while she rides the bus across the city. She is single and used to managing on her own. Her friends describe her as disciplined, funny, and hard to pin down, always leaving one rehearsal for another, always carrying a canvas bag with water, tape, and an extra pair of shoes.

The attack happens on an ordinary afternoon. She is in a crowded public plaza on her way to teach a youth dance class. She remembers hearing a burst of noise that does not make sense at first, then a shock wave that seems to strike through her chest and legs. In her memory, time changes shape. There is the metallic smell, screaming, fragments of glass, a shoe lying alone on the pavement, and the strange thought that she needs to protect her hands because she is supposed to teach that evening. She drops to the ground without deciding to, then runs when other people run. Later she learns it is a terrorist attack. At the time, all she knows is that people are bleeding, someone is calling for help, and her own body is moving automatically while her mind feels split off and far behind.

In the first days afterward, she tells herself she is lucky. She survives with bruises and a cut along one arm. News coverage loops constantly on screens in cafés, on phones, in studio lobbies. Each replay catches her off guard, and she feels the blast again in her ribs. She stops watching, but images still find her. At night she jerks awake sweating, convinced she hears another explosion. Sometimes in the half-second after waking she cannot tell whether she is in her apartment or back in the plaza with dust in her mouth. She begins sleeping with the lights on because darkness makes the memories sharper.

She returns to the studio quickly because dance is the only way she knows to reclaim her body. At first she thinks movement will settle her. Instead, certain sounds—bass vibrations, a door slamming in the hallway, the sharp crack of a speaker—send panic through her so suddenly that she has to grip the barre to stay upright. During combinations she loses count and stares into space while the rest of the group keeps going. She becomes ashamed of how easily she startles. Her body, once reliable, now feels like it belongs to fear. She notices exits in every room and positions herself near them. On the train she scans faces, bags, hands. If someone leaves a backpack unattended, her throat tightens and she gets off at the next stop, even if it means walking for an hour.

Friends invite her out, but crowded places feel unbearable. She turns down festivals, performances, even small dinners if the restaurant is busy. She tells people she is tired or overworked. Being single had once felt like freedom; now her apartment feels too quiet, yet having anyone close feels impossible. When people ask where she was that day, she either gives a flat, rehearsed answer or changes the subject. A few times she tries to talk about it, but the words snag on the details she cannot control: the smell, the sound, the sight of bodies on the ground. She worries that if she starts, she will not stop.

Months pass, and her world narrows. She is still teaching and dancing, but only just. She arrives early so she can check the building. She is irritable with students when they fool around near the mirrors or drop props with a bang. She hates this version of herself immediately afterward and sometimes cries in the staff bathroom, furious that children’s laughter can feel like a threat when it rises too suddenly. On the street she is constantly braced, shoulders lifted, jaw clenched, as if impact is always one second away. Exhaustion settles into her, but rest does not help. Her mind keeps returning to the attack in flashes she does not invite: a stranger’s hand reaching toward her, dust floating in sunlight, the stunned silence after the initial blast before the screaming fully begins.

What disturbs her most is how the trauma enters dance itself. Music used to open her up; now she sometimes hears danger in the crescendo. Choreography that asks for surrender, stillness, or falling to the floor makes her pulse race. She used to inhabit performance as a place of expression. Now when an audience coughs, shifts, or rustles in the dark, part of her remains on alert, tracking every sound. She can still execute the steps, but she often feels absent inside them, as if she is watching herself from a distance.

In sessions, she speaks carefully at first, then with more grief than she expects. She says she misses the person who could move through the city without calculating escape routes. She misses spontaneity, trust, and the simple pleasure of being in a crowd because it meant life was happening around her. She keeps dancing because it is the clearest language she has, but even there, terror has left its imprint. Her days are now shaped by avoidance, vigilance, broken sleep, and the effort of holding herself together in a body that no longer feels fully safe.
